# Railroads and the First California Monopoly {#sec-2-09}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Land, Monopoly, and Institution · 1862–1869
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does infrastructure become sovereignty?

**The answer.** By owning the only way through. The Central Pacific took federal
land grants and federal bonds, built with Chinese labour it paid least and
credited not at all, and emerged owning the sole rail connection between
California and the rest of the country. The golden spike is not the completion
of a public work. It is the ceremony at which a public work becomes a private
monopoly.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, in the book's
clearest single instance. Federal land grants and bonds financed the line; a
construction company owned by the same four men captured the margin; and the
resulting entity priced the movement of every good in the state.

**The key fact.** Leland Stanford was Governor of California while the Central
Pacific was being organised, advocating the railroad as a public necessity while
holding its presidency. There was no conflict-of-interest framework to violate;
the roles were simply held at once.

**The human anchor.** Stanford, in both offices at once. And against him, the
Chinese crews on the Sierra grade, working through winters in snow tunnels,
whose names are almost entirely absent from a record that carefully preserves
the names of the four men who hired them.

**Excluded voices.** The Chinese workforce, at its peak the overwhelming
majority of the Central Pacific's labour, paid less than white workers, housed
worse, and killed in numbers the company did not trouble to count. The 1867
strike belongs here. So does the near-total absence of these men from the
Promontory photograph.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that public money built the private fortune at
the root of the Stanford endowment by showing the land grants, the bond terms,
and the construction-company mechanism that captured them.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** The Promontory photograph, and who is not in it. Open on the
   absence.
2. **The Big Four.** Stanford, Huntington, Hopkins, Crocker: four Sacramento
   merchants, not engineers. What each actually did. They are the shovel-sellers
   of ch. 6, scaled up.
3. **Judah, used and discarded.** The engineer who made it possible and was
   bought out. His death in 1863.
4. **The subsidy.** Land grants and bonds, in specific figures, per mile and by
   terrain. This is public money and the chapter must make the reader feel its
   size.
5. **The Contract and Finance Company.** The construction company owned by the
   same four men, contracting with the railroad the same four men controlled.
   The margin captured at the point of transfer. Flag it as the manoeuvre that
   recurs in Act IV ch. 7.
6. **Stanford in two chairs.** Governor and president of the railroad. Advocate
   and beneficiary.
7. **The Chinese workforce.** Recruitment, numbers, pay differential, the Sierra
   grade, the snow tunnels, deaths. The 1867 strike and its suppression.
8. **Completion, 10 May 1869.** The ceremony, and what it transferred.
9. **What the monopoly then did.** Rates. Whoever owns the rails sets the prices
   — the sentence from Act I, now with a California address.
10. **Landing.** A federally financed private monopoly, held by four men, one of
   whom will spend a portion of it on a university. Hand off to ch. 10: how they
   made it permanent.
:::
